statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that cannot be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about 1 to 2 hours before death, every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences to drug diffusing out of organs after death, but no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) found, where the same case had both values, median ratios to femoral blood across drugs of 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs for most specimens (for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no range or interval is given for any ratio, and cause of death and time since death could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 studies selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that the first sample in these human studies was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so earlier change was not seen. It gives no sizes, does not appraise the studies, judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio shows that change after death occurred but not how much, and concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs without case numbers or sources (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3), higher than the compilation's paired medians for several of the same drugs (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or lower, for drugs that break down or are lost after death. The evidence consists of selected case series, an unappraised compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In bodies examined after death, the amount of a drug was often different depending on which blood vessel the blood came from: in four overdose deaths, from about 3 to 7 times, usually higher near the heart, lungs and liver than in the thigh. In one person tested in hospital before death, every sample taken after death was about 2 to 8 times higher. In about 5,000 cases collected from many studies, blood from other sites, such as the heart, held on average about a quarter more drug than thigh blood, with big differences between drugs. Levels in thigh blood also rose or fell in the hours after death for some drugs, and the first sample was often taken many hours after death. So a level after death can make a drug look more, or less, involved than it was. Most of this comes from small or selected studies, mostly of medicines.

risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, without appraisal, weighting or spread (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). indirectness.note: The question concerns deaths involving any drug, including drugs used outside medicine; the compilation excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids, the case series concerns large overdoses of medicines with drug still in the gut, and part of the evidence on timing is from animals.

imprecision.note: Four cases; no ranges, percentiles or intervals for any compiled ratio; many drug–specimen ratios rest on one to three results.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for case series and compilations of case literature.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

statement: A drug concentration measured after death cannot on its own show that the drug caused the death: concentrations in deaths put down to a drug overlap with those in deaths from other causes and with those measured in living patients taking the drug as a treatment, tolerance shifts the level a person can survive, and levels change after death (see the answer on whether levels change after death). In Finland, where police can order a medico-legal investigation of a sudden or unexplained death and the forensic pathologist decides whether to test for drugs (over 13% of all deaths), one laboratory measured femoral-blood levels in 57,903 deaths of all causes with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, sampled on average five days after death; for 46 of 129 drugs the median level was above the range measured in living patients' plasma during treatment, by up to 100-fold, for 61 it was within that range and for 22 below it. The median for methadone (207 deaths) and for buprenorphine (671 deaths) lay within the treatment range although forensic pathologists certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings by that drug, and the authors state that for strong opioids the level after death plays a limited part in judging the cause, because of tolerance; the medians mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out levels too low to measure, and compare whole blood with plasma ranges (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). In 77 deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England (1992 to 2008), femoral-blood MDMA overlapped widely between deaths put down to MDMA (0.478 to 53.9 mg/L in 13 with a value) and deaths from injuries (0.035 to 4.81 mg/L in 24), although the median was about 7 times higher in the first group (editors' calculation; Milroy, 2011; see the answer on MDMA levels). A 1977 Michigan series, as a 1996 narrative review describes it, found blood morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes, such as injuries or homicide, in 74% of deaths put down to heroin overdose (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand; see the answer on heroin 'overdoses'). A clinical pharmacologist's review adds, second-hand, that published 'lethal' ranges are wide and overlap (for example 40 to 8,500 µg/L quoted for MDMA and 60 to 3,100 µg/L for methadone), that amounts that would kill a person without tolerance are survived by people who use heroin regularly, and that a fatal level could only be defined by classing deaths as caused by the drug or not without knowing the measured levels and then comparing the two groups (Ferner, 2008), which none of the studies read here did; a 2003 practitioners' review lists nine questions a toxicologist should answer before judging a drug's role, among them where the blood was taken, whether the drug changes after death, what is known of the person's tolerance and whether the autopsy findings fit (Leikin & Watson, 2003). Both directions follow: a level that looks high can lead to a death being put down to a drug that was only present, and an ordinary or low level does not rule a drug out. At one North Carolina centre that kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths (2016 to 2021), 265 of 2,719 deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug deaths (9.75%) were given a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology, some with drugs present and some with none found (the split is not reported), while 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were judged drug deaths; the pathologists counted any illicit drug found as at least contributing unless a catastrophic other cause was found (Hancock et al., 2024; see the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing). In these studies the people who decided the cause of death knew the measured levels, and none compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can a blood test after death show that a drug caused the death? Not on its own. In Finland, in about 58,000 deaths tested for drugs (2000 to 2010), the usual level after death was higher than the treatment level in living patients for 46 of 129 drugs. For methadone and buprenorphine the usual level was in the treatment range, even though more than 4 in 10 of those deaths were counted as poisonings by that drug, and people who use heroin regularly can survive amounts that would kill someone without tolerance. In an English study, MDMA levels in deaths blamed on MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries, and an old US study found the same for morphine in deaths blamed on heroin. So a high level can lead to a death being blamed on a drug that was only there, and a normal level does not rule a drug out. At one US centre, about 1 in 10 deaths suspected to be drug deaths had another cause after a full autopsy, while about half of the deaths not suspected turned out to be drug deaths. The doctors who decided the causes knew the levels.

North Carolina 2016–2021: 265/2,719 (9.75%) suspected drug deaths with a non-drug final cause; 115/237 (48.5%, editors' calculation) of deaths not suspected judged drug deaths. No intervals.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and in the one large autopsy registry read here no death was certified as a poisoning by THC, the main active substance of cannabis. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with no stated selection rules or appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that no minimum blood THC level can show cause because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). They relay, second-hand, studies pointing both ways: a heart-attack risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people, and a higher death rate after a heart attack with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14, in 1,913 people), against no association with death from heart disease in 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years, and two systematic reviews that disagree; the review's statement that eleven of its twelve tabulated studies showed raised risk is not borne out by its own table (Drummer et al., 2019). In Finland, among 57,903 medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, THC was found in femoral blood in 347 deaths (median 0.002 mg/L, that is 2 ng/mL), and forensic pathologists certified none of them as a fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). THC levels after death are hard to read: THC in femoral blood fell after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026, relayed without sizes), and whole blood, the usual post-mortem sample, has to be multiplied by about 1.6 to compare with the plasma values used for living people (Leikin & Watson, 2003, second-hand). The case reports have no comparison group and cannot show how often THC is present in sudden deaths that cannabis did not cause, so counting cannabis as a cause on the reviewers' criteria would rest on THC being present plus the circumstances. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Can cannabis cause death? In the studies read here, no death was put down to cannabis poisoning alone: in Finland, none of 347 people who died with THC in their blood (2000 to 2010) was counted as a THC poisoning. Published reports describe 13 men who died suddenly soon after using cannabis, mostly from heart problems; 8 already had heart disease or other illness, alcohol was found in 2, and 5 had no blood test showing recent use. Whether cannabis caused these deaths cannot be shown. Studies of heart attacks point both ways: one found more heart attacks in the hour after smoking cannabis, while a 25-year study found no link with heart deaths. Some deaths have also been put down to a severe vomiting illness linked to cannabis, but no numbers are given. The forensic doctors who wrote the review want cannabis counted as a contributing cause in such deaths and think deaths are missed, but give no numbers. See the contested question.

debate.question: Can using cannabis cause a sudden death, for example by setting off a heart attack or a dangerous heart rhythm, and should such deaths be counted as cannabis deaths?
debate.evidence_yes: Case reports describe 13 men aged 17 to 52 whose deaths their authors linked to recent cannabis use, 8 of them with THC measured in blood (1.9 to 22 ng/mL) and five described as having little obvious heart disease; in one case a coroner found cannabis a secondary cause of death (Drummer et al., 2019). The same review describes 35 people in 31 case reports who reached hospital with heart attacks (18 confirmed by blood tests), rhythm problems or strokes during or soon after cannabis use, 24 of them without evidence of coronary artery disease (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, a case-crossover study of 3,882 people with a heart attack found a risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis; among 1,913 people after a heart attack the death rate was higher with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14); in national hospital data ischaemic stroke was more common (adjusted risk ratio 1.17, 1.15 to 1.20); among 2,097 people with a heart attack before age 51, cardiovascular death was more common (adjusted hazard ratio 2.22, printed as a 90% CI of 1.27 to 3.70); and a systematic review of 81 case reports and 29 observational studies found an association with cardiovascular disease, stronger for ischaemic stroke (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without numbers, deaths attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (Drummer et al., 2019). The forensic reviewers hold that a small number of susceptible people with other illnesses could be harmed, and that when use was very recent, blood THC is positive and the death could be cardiac or cerebrovascular, cannabis should be recorded as at least a contributory cause so that its harm is not underestimated (Drummer et al., 2019).
debate.evidence_no: In the Finnish autopsy registry, none of 347 deaths with THC in femoral blood in 2000 to 2010 was certified as a THC poisoning (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Of the 13 published deaths, 8 had significant coronary disease or other pathology, alcohol was found in 2 (blood alcohol 0.04% and 0.119%), 5 lacked the blood THC result that the reviewers themselves require to link a death to recent use, one had no THC in blood, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers state that the link with death from heart disease is not clear, that the events described may have other causes such as undiagnosed rhythm disorders or tobacco smoking, and that the risk is probably rare (Drummer et al., 2019). As relayed, the CARDIA cohort of 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years found no association of cannabis use with cardiovascular death; a cohort of 3,886 people followed for 18 years found 29% higher mortality with cannabis use that was not statistically significant; and a systematic review found no compelling evidence linking cannabis use with death, including from heart attack (Drummer et al., 2019). The review's count of eleven of twelve studies showing raised risk is not borne out by its own table, in which at most 8 rows report a raised estimate, some not significant (first reader's reading of Drummer et al., 2019).
debate.neither_can_show: Case reports are published because someone suspected a link; deaths with THC present that were judged unrelated go unpublished, so the reports cannot show how often a link is real or how often THC is found in sudden deaths in general, and they have no comparison group. THC in blood after death does not show when cannabis was used or how much: no minimum level marks recent use or cause, laboratories detect down to 1 to 2 ng/mL, low values may reflect use days earlier, THC levels change after death, and whole blood differs from the serum used for living values (Drummer et al., 2019; Borra et al., 2026; Leikin & Watson, 2003). Certification in the registry rests on pathologists' judgment without stated criteria, so a death set off by cannabis could be put down to heart disease, and a death in which cannabis was only present could be put down to cannabis. The epidemiological studies rely mostly on self-reported use or hospital coding, are known here only second-hand, and measure heart attacks and strokes more often than deaths.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the sources read, no death was put down to cannabis poisoning on its own. The deaths linked to cannabis are a small number of sudden heart or brain-vessel deaths soon after use, mostly in men who already had heart disease, sometimes with alcohol, and several without a blood test showing recent use. Whether cannabis set off any of them cannot be shown from case reports, and the population studies relayed by the review point both ways, mostly for heart attacks rather than deaths. The forensic reviewers' call to count cannabis as a contributory cause, and their view that such deaths are undercounted, are positions without data on how many deaths are missed or on how often THC is present in deaths it did not cause; applied in certification, they would raise counts of cannabis deaths on the strength of THC being present plus the circumstances.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A population-based study of sudden cardiac deaths with complete toxicology (blood THC with the time from death to sampling recorded), compared with suitable controls such as deaths from external causes or living people from the same population, with coronary disease, tobacco and alcohol measured, to estimate whether recent cannabis use raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and how often THC is present in such deaths without having contributed; and agreement studies of certification rules for drug contribution, tested on pathologists who do not know the toxicology results.

statement: Deaths recorded as heroin 'overdoses' often involve other drugs, delays and other mechanisms, so the label does not show that heroin alone caused the death, but which substance or mechanism was decisive in a given death cannot be read from the toxicology. In a 1996 narrative review of medical examiners' and coroners' series and official statistics, mostly from 1967 to 1996 in the USA, Australia and Europe, chosen by the authors without a stated search and leaning on their own New South Wales series of 152 heroin-related deaths in 1992, morphine (the substance heroin becomes in the body) was the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% to 48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose across six studies; alcohol was detected in 29% to 75% across 13 studies, with mean blood alcohol of 0.09 to 0.16 g/100 mL where reported, and benzodiazepines in 12% to 55% across four; which drugs each laboratory looked for, and how each source defined a heroin death, is not given (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). Blood morphine was lower in deaths with alcohol in the five studies that compared them, with weak correlations where reported (r = −0.14 in 505 deaths; r = −0.28 in the authors' series); a third of the authors' series had morphine below the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L); and a 1977 Michigan series found 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes (Darke & Zador, 1996). Many deaths were not instant: 14% of the authors' series were classed as instant and 22% took more than 3 hours, other series found intervals of more than 2 or 3 hours in 44% and 52%, and other people were present at more than half of the deaths in four studies (58% to 79% where a figure was given; Darke & Zador, 1996). The reviewers write that 'overdose' 'may correctly apply to only a minority of heroin-related deaths' and propose 'multiple drug toxicity' for many of them; but finding other drugs does not show that they caused the death, the comparison with survivors rests on three studies cited without figures, tolerance was measured in no study, and low morphine can also reflect a death hours after the last injection, when morphine had already fallen, or change after death (Darke & Zador, 1996). In England and Wales in 2000, of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths that coroners reported to a national register (the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths; reporting voluntary, coverage not stated), the register's researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct overdoses and 235 (23%) as other mechanisms: choking on stomach contents and other acute events (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18). Heroin or morphine was named as implicated in 424 of the direct overdoses and found after death in 488, and was implicated in 42 of the 74 acute events, 33 of the 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition and 11 of the 18 infections; alcohol was found after death in 316 (39.4%) of the direct overdoses; methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses but was the only drug implicated in 4%. These figures are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns that recorded only drugs found, not a check of official statistics, which were not compared (Webb et al., 2003). In the other direction, heroin can be missed: 6-MAM, the marker that shows heroin rather than another source of morphine, fell in femoral blood after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026), and a review table reports, second-hand, that testing the fluid around the brain and spinal cord for 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related deaths than testing blood (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The evidence is old (before fentanyl), largely second-hand, and from series chosen by the authors or from a register. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are deaths called heroin 'overdoses' always caused by heroin alone? Often not, but tests after death cannot show which drug mattered most. In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe (1967 to 1996), heroin (found as morphine) was the only drug found in about 23 to 48 in 100 deaths called heroin overdoses. Alcohol was found in about 29 to 75 in 100, and sleeping or calming pills (benzodiazepines) in 12 to 55 in 100. Many people did not die at once: in one series, about 1 in 5 took more than 3 hours to die, and other people were often there. Heroin can also be missed, because its marker breaks down after death. These studies are old, from before fentanyl.

statement: In the UK, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man, of 128 deaths alleged by October 2011 to be linked to mephedrone, mephedrone was not found after death in 25 (about 1 in 5) and results were still awaited for 13; of the 90 with mephedrone found, inquests had concluded for 69 and 62 were analysed, and in these 62 mephedrone was the only substance found in 8 and was named in the recorded cause of death in 36, on its own in 18 (Schifano et al., 2012). Deaths entered the count as allegations, from a national register at St George's, University of London, that receives information on drug-related deaths from coroners and, in Scotland, procurators fiscal (the National Programme on Substance Abuse Deaths), from internet searches of toxicology, newspaper and media websites, and from a toxicology group; media reports filled gaps where coroners' files could not be seen. The register admits a death if a drug was directly implicated, the person had a history of drug dependence or misuse, or a controlled drug was found after death, so a death could enter because mephedrone was present (Schifano et al., 2012). A 'confirmed' death meant that mephedrone was identified, not that it caused the death, as the authors state; one of the 62, who died in hospital three weeks after taking it, had none found after death. Other substances were found in 54 of the 62, most often alcohol (26), other stimulants (22) and sleeping or calming medicines (22); by the authors' grouping, 26 deaths were drug poisonings with mephedrone alone or with other substances, 18 were self-inflicted (11 by hanging), 6 followed risky behaviour such as trying to swim a river, driving or a stabbing, 5 followed collapse at a party, 5 occurred in hospital days or weeks later and 2 followed risky sexual activity; the coroners' or procurators fiscal's verdicts were accident or misadventure in 35, suicide in 11, open in 8, 'abuse of drugs' in 5 and homicide, natural causes and a narrative verdict in 1 each (Schifano et al., 2012). In the other direction, the authors call the count a minimum: about 95% of coroners' areas in England and Wales report regularly, a test may fail to detect mephedrone, and deaths in which it was not tested for or not alleged are not counted (Schifano et al., 2012). Who decided that mephedrone was part of the cause, and on what evidence, is not stated; the laboratories, specimens and tests are not described; and with no count of people using mephedrone, no death rate can be given. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

statement: 'Excited delirium' is a contested label rather than a recognized diagnosis, and evidence is insufficient to say whether the state it describes kills without restraint, or how far deaths given the label were caused by restraint, by drugs such as cocaine, or by both. It is not in the international classification of diseases (ICD) or the psychiatric manual (DSM), has no validated diagnostic criteria and no autopsy or laboratory finding specific to it, and is applied as a diagnosis of exclusion, mainly in medico-legal reports of deaths of agitated people during or after police restraint or in custody (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020). In the published case literature the label was used mostly by forensic pathologists, and also by emergency physicians and others, and a 2012 defining review and a 2009 emergency physicians' white paper gave fatality figures for it (under 10% and 8.3%) that the authors of the pooled analysis below trace to a study without any death figures (Strömmer et al., 2020). The authors of both reviews read here reject the term: one team proposes 'agitated delirium' with a note of the presence and degree of restraint, and recording the manner of death of restrained people as homicide or undetermined rather than natural or accident (Strömmer et al., 2020); the other uses 'acute behavioral disturbance' and reports critics' view that the label deflects attention from restraint and is applied with racial bias (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). In a pooled analysis of 168 published cases (English-language case reports and series to April 2020), 92 of 120 cases labelled 'excited delirium' had died, against 12 of 48 labelled 'agitated delirium'; some force, from manual restraint and handcuffs to electrical weapons or sedation, was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths, only 3 of the 168 cases had no force recorded (2 of them died), and cocaine was noted in 55 of the 104 deaths and 19 of the 64 survivors, as the case reports described it rather than as toxicology results (Strömmer et al., 2020). Its authors read this as no evidence that excited delirium kills without restraint; but their own introduction notes that forensic reports describe deaths and use 'excited delirium' while clinical reports describe survivors, so the label, death and the recording of restraint travel together by type of source, which the analysis did not take into account, and the authors later corrected one table (Strömmer et al., 2020, and the first reader's appraisal). A 2026 systematic review of deaths in custody (searches for 2010 to 2025) describes restraint deaths mostly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and stimulant intoxication, names cocaine, methamphetamine and phencyclidine as 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' without figures, favours breathing restriction and metabolic collapse during face-down restraint over a heart-rhythm death driven by stimulants while allowing the latter in some deaths, and reports, without figures, that restraint-related deaths are under-recorded in official statistics; in one Ontario series of 46 investigation reports, most deaths were classified as accidental or natural (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). Both reviews are rated critically low for their methods, neither counts how often drugs caused or contributed to these deaths, and neither can show the cause of any single death. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What is 'excited delirium', and why is it disputed? It is a label used mostly in reports of deaths, for extreme agitation in people who die during or after being held down, often by police, and often with drugs such as cocaine or methamphetamine present. It is not an official diagnosis, has no agreed definition and leaves no specific sign at autopsy. In 168 published cases, some force, such as being held down, handcuffs or sedation, was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths; only 3 cases had no force recorded. Some researchers say the label hides deaths caused by restraint and want it dropped; others hold that the agitated state, often with stimulant drugs, can be fatal in itself. The published cases are selected, and the evidence cannot show what caused any single death. See the contested question.

No counts of drug involvement.

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews are critically low under AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_strommer_2020 and sc_goncalves_dias_2026): the pooled cases are selected for publication, the label, outcome and recording of restraint depend on the type of source, nearly half of the cases come from seven articles, nothing is adjusted, and the extraction is disputed in a published critique; the 2026 review does not identify most of its included studies and draws its mechanism mainly from reviews by one author and series selected through litigation.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews, and the evidence within them, are read in opposite ways: deaths labelled 'excited delirium' as restraint deaths, or as deaths from an agitated state and stimulant drugs in which restraint is incidental.

indirectness.note: Case reports and death series are not a sample of people in severe agitation; volunteer experiments cannot reproduce agitation, exhaustion, obesity and stimulant intoxication; drugs are as described in case reports, not measured.

imprecision.note: Only 3 of 168 cases had no force recorded; no denominators of encounters; drug involvement is not counted.

publication_bias.note: Not separately rated; selection for publication is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one each for inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Counted once: the 2026 review cites the pooled analysis (its ref. 32) for its multifactorial reading, so the two are not independent on that point. Status contested: credible readings and critiques point both ways, so the six-part debate box applies. The claim names who uses the term and who rejects it, from these two reviews; statements by professional bodies withdrawing support for the term (reports on the death-counting list) were not read.

debate.question: Is 'excited delirium' a condition that can kill on its own, often together with stimulant drugs, or a label that hides deaths caused mainly by restraint?
debate.evidence_yes: Those who use the term describe deaths in extreme agitation, often with stimulants, in which autopsy finds no anatomical cause and drug levels are usually in the range seen with recreational use rather than in fatal poisonings, so the death is explained by the state itself (as described by Strömmer et al., 2020). In the pooled published cases, 2 deaths had no force recorded, and the 2026 review notes that deaths attributed to the syndrome may occur without overt restraint (Strömmer et al., 2020; Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). Experiments in healthy volunteers found that face-down and weighted restraint reduced lung volumes and increased the work of breathing without clinically significant lack of oxygen or major circulatory effects, spit hoods made no clinically significant difference to oxygen levels, and in simulated arrests intense exertion disturbed body chemistry more than electrical weapons, sprays or police dogs; prospective studies of police use of force occasionally report low death rates (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). The 2026 review itself allows that surges of stress hormones with stimulant intoxication may set off fatal heart rhythms in some deaths, and cocaine was noted more often in the pooled deaths (55 of 104) than in survivors (19 of 64), unadjusted (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026; Strömmer et al., 2020).
debate.evidence_no: In the 168 pooled published cases, the 'excited delirium' label went with death (92 of 120, against 12 of 48 for 'agitated delirium'), with police rather than paramedics first on the scene (95 of 120 against 16 of 48), and with handcuffs (80 against 6) and hog or hobble ties (46 against 1), while 'agitated delirium' went with sedation (30 of 48 against 16 of 120); some force was recorded in 94 of the 104 deaths and only 3 cases had none recorded; the share of published cases that were fatal fell from 90% of the 30 published before 2000 to 56% of the 138 published from 2000 to 2020, which the authors attribute to awareness of restraint asphyxia; and they trace published fatality figures of under 10% and 8.3% to a study without death figures (Strömmer et al., 2020). The 2026 review finds no validated criteria and no specific autopsy or molecular finding (a stress protein proposed as a marker was found in people who used cocaine whatever the label), reports critics' view that the label deflects attention from restraint and is racially biased, cites a review of 229 deaths in which 58% occurred within 1 to 5 minutes of starting face-down restraint and breathing distress was recorded in at least 20% before collapse, and reports, from reviews by one author, that the final heart rhythms in such deaths are mostly not the kind expected from a stimulant-driven arrhythmia; in one Ontario series of 46 reports most deaths were classified as accidental or natural, and restraint-related deaths are said to be under-recorded in official statistics (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: There is no agreed case definition, so who is counted depends on who applies the label. In the pooled analysis, the label, the outcome and how fully restraint was recorded all depend on whether a case came from a forensic series of deaths or a clinical report of survivors; cases were selected for publication, nearly half came from seven articles, nothing was adjusted, and with only 3 cases without recorded force the risk of death without restraint cannot be estimated (Strömmer et al., 2020). Breathing, position, the duration and force of restraint and blood drug levels were not measured in the pooled cases, and drugs were taken from case descriptions rather than toxicology (Strömmer et al., 2020). Volunteer experiments cannot reproduce agitation, exhaustion, obesity, stimulant intoxication and a prolonged struggle; the death series cited for rapid collapse were partly selected through civil litigation; the 2026 review does not identify most of the studies behind its statements; and where death investigators depend on police or prison authorities, classification may be biased (Gonçalves Dias & Cainé, 2026). None of this evidence can show what caused any single death, and none counts how often drugs contributed.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). 'Excited delirium' names a picture of extreme agitation that police, pathologists and emergency physicians describe, often with stimulant drugs such as cocaine or methamphetamine present, but it is not a recognized diagnosis, has no agreed definition and leaves no specific trace at autopsy, so calling a death 'excited delirium' records a description, not a cause. In the published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths and was recorded as absent in only 3 of 168 cases, so this literature cannot show whether the state kills without restraint; it cannot show that restraint caused a particular death either, because breathing, position and force were not measured and the cases were selected. How much stimulant drugs contribute is not measured in either review. Both reviews call for complete autopsy with toxicology, a detailed record of the restraint and investigation independent of the custodial authority in every such death; the evidence read supports these as ways to answer the question, not a verdict on it.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A prospective register, or linked police, ambulance, hospital and death-investigation records across several places, covering every encounter with a person in severe agitation, fatal or not, with one case definition applied without knowing the outcome, and recording restraint type, position, duration and compression, devices, sedation, the first heart rhythm, body temperature, blood gases and blood drug concentrations, with full autopsy by investigators independent of the custodial authority; in the meantime, a re-analysis of the published cases that takes the type of source and the clustering of cases within articles into account.
